extracted.intended_audience: regulated industry (power plant owners/operators and manufacturers), environmental regulators, policy analysts, and environmental/energy legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: EPA preamble guidance for determining the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) and promulgating phased standards of performance under CAA section 111(b) for new and reconstructed combined-cycle (base load and intermediate load) combustion turbines, including evaluation of highly efficient generation and CCS pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately Demonstrated (legal test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The system (not the standard) must be adequately demonstrated and the standard must be achievable; sufficient evidence must exist to reasonably determine that affected sources can adopt the specific system to achieve the specified degree of emission limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted framing: “it is the system which must be adequately demonstrated and the standard which must be achievable.” The Agency may extrapolate demonstration data from similar sources (citing Lignite Energy Council v. EPA). Lead time may be accommodated per D.C. Circuit caselaw. Evaluation should consider capture, transport, and sequestration components together when assessing adequate demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of Costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards of performance must reflect systems that can be implemented at reasonable cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA assessed capital vs. fuel costs: e.g., high-efficiency combined cycle capital costs ~1.9% higher but fuel use ~2.6% lower; capital recovered at capacity factors ≥40% over a 30-year facility life. For CCS, recent cost declines and policies (e.g., IRC section 45Q tax credit) factor into reasonableness. Consider lifecycle capital, fixed, operating costs, and potential offsets (fuel savings, tax credits) in the cost evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Air Quality Health and Environmental Impacts and Energy Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the control technology has significant adverse non-air quality health or environmental impacts or significant adverse energy requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA found highly efficient generation reduces non-air quality impacts and energy requirements because less fuel is needed to produce the same output. For CCS, adverse impacts and energy penalties can often be mitigated; the energy requirements must not be unreasonably adverse. Assess solvent degradation, fouling, additional pretreatment needs, and mitigation options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of Emissions Reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the magnitude of emission reductions achievable by the proposed BSER and quantify reductions where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA used a methodology to estimate CO2 reductions (e.g., setting the base load standard at 800 lb CO2/MWh-gross, identifying units above that rate, estimating reductions to the standard at observed capacity factors, and averaging across years). EPA provided numeric estimates (e.g., annual reductions of 313,000 short tons CO2 initially, growing to 939,000 tons in year 3) and also estimated NOx co-benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of Development and Implementation of Technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether selecting a technology as the BSER will promote broader penetration and development of improved control technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA reasoned that designating highly efficient generation as BSER would advance penetration of best-performing turbines and incentivize manufacturers to offer improved turbines that meet the standard, providing additional support for the BSER determination beyond the basic statutory factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority for Multi-Component (Phased) BSER and Lead Time
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(b) authorizes EPA to determine BSER as a set of controls with multiple components and to promulgate phased standards of performance with differing compliance dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards may be effective upon promulgation while compliance obligations are phased (EPA may provide lead time for later components). D.C. Circuit caselaw permits considering lead time within the 'adequately demonstrated' analysis. EPA cited past rulemakings establishing phased or stepped compliance approaches as precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards Effective Upon Promulgation with Phased Compliance Deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards of performance become effective when promulgated, but compliance obligations can be phased such that different components must be met by different dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affected sources are legally subject to the multi-phase standard upon promulgation; they must comply with first-phase standards upon initial startup and with second-phase standards by specified future dates (e.g., EPA finalized first-phase compliance at startup and second-phase compliance beginning January 2032). This is distinct from '8-year review' revisions which apply to sources commencing construction after the revision proposal date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology Neutrality and Compliance Pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards of performance are technology-neutral; affected sources may comply using any means that achieve the standard even if EPA did not designate that technology as the BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although EPA did not finalize low-GHG hydrogen co-firing as the BSER, affected sources may nevertheless comply by co-firing hydrogen because the standard itself is technology-neutral. EPA evaluated hydrogen pathways but did not finalize them as BSER components due to record-based reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly Efficient Generation as BSER for Base Load Combustion Turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of highly efficient combined-cycle generation in combination with best operating and maintenance practices is a component (first component) of the BSER for new and reconstructed base load combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA found such designs are adequately demonstrated (decades of use), commercially available, achievable, and in many cases cost-neutral or cost-reducing over life-cycle due to fuel savings. EPA set first-phase performance reflecting this BSER (e.g., 800 lb CO2/MWh-gross for base load). Consider differences for smaller turbines (<2,000 MMBtu/h) and less stringent subcategory standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: CCS with 90% Capture as a BSER Component for Base Load Combustion Turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: Carbon capture and sequestration with 90 percent CO2 capture is a component of the BSER for new base load combined-cycle combustion turbines (second component).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA determined CCS (capture + transport + sequestration) is adequately demonstrated, achieves substantial reductions, is widely applicable, and can be implemented at reasonable cost in light of cost declines and incentives (e.g., 45Q). EPA addressed and weighed non-air impacts and energy penalties and cited international and domestic demonstration/planned projects supporting adequacy (Bellingham, TCM, Peterhead, Sutter, Deer Park, Baytown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical Considerations for CO2 Capture on Natural Gas Combined Cycle (NGCC) vs Coal
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for differences in flue gas composition and CO2 concentration when assessing capture feasibility and design of capture systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural gas-fired combined cycle flue gas has lower CO2 concentration (~3–4 vol%) and far fewer impurities (SO2, PM, metals) than coal (~13–15 vol%), which reduces fouling and solvent degradation concerns. Lower CO2 concentration is manageable through correct sizing and design of capture equipment; amine solvents can remove CO2 to below atmospheric concentrations. HRSGs are integral to cooling flue gas prior to capture. Oxy-combustion (e.g., NET Power) provides an alternative by producing pipeline-quality CO2 without solvent capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Demonstrations, Vendor Experience, and Project Pipeline Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess adequacy of technologies using operational history, vendor commercial deployments, and pipeline of planned projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA relied on long-running demonstrations (e.g., Bellingham capture 1991–2005 with 85–95% capture and 98.5% availability), vendor technologies with multi-decade operation (Fluor Econamine FG Plus), test centers (TCM), planned large projects (Peterhead, Sutter, Deer Park, Baytown), and industry trackers (Global CCS Centre) to support adequacy and achievability findings. Project design details (quencher/absorber/stripper columns, air permits) and expected capture rates (95%+) were cited as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Technical Limit to High Capture from Dilute Flue Gases (Engineering Achievability)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no technical limit preventing high-percentage CO2 removal from dilute flue gases; appropriate engineering can achieve targeted capture rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes amine-based solvents have been shown to remove CO2 from low-concentration streams and that design/sizing can address lower driving forces. Differences between coal and gas streams introduce different engineering challenges (e.g., pretreatment for coal), but in many respects gas-fired CCS is simpler and may face fewer solvent degradation/fouling issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and Rejection of Alternative BSER Pathways (Hydrogen, Lower-Emitting Fuels)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considered alternative second-component pathways (e.g., co-firing low-GHG hydrogen, lower-emitting fuels) but did not finalize them as BSER components where the record showed insufficient emission reductions or other issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For base load turbines, lower-emitting fuels would achieve few emission reductions compared to highly efficient generation ± CCS and thus were not finalized; EPA proposed but did not finalize hydrogen co-firing pathways for various reasons explained elsewhere in the preamble. Nonetheless, technology-neutral standards allow these alternatives to be used for compliance if they achieve the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with Policy Incentives (e.g., IRC section 45Q) in Cost Assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of cost-effectiveness and reasonableness of CCS includes interaction with existing or anticipated policy incentives such as the federal 45Q tax credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA found CCS implementation costs are reasonable in light of recent cost declines and the availability of incentives (45Q), which improve the economic case for CCS and were explicitly considered in the BSER cost analysis.
